LESSON 32 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Random Numbers, Nonces and Weak Entropy

Cryptography fails quietly when randomness is predictable: where entropy comes from, the exact job a nonce does, and how a crippled generator destroys key strength.

Foundation12 min
Why this matters

Much of modern security depends on values nobody should be able to predict. Weak randomness in the wrong place does not reduce security slightly; it removes it completely for that mechanism.

Tracing how untrusted strings reach browser rendering sinks and how context-aware encoding neutralizes execution.

  1. Source: User submits profile text, search query, or URL fragment.

01 Markup / Event Payload

03 Script Execution
  1. Source: Attacker supplies HTML tags, event attributes, or a javascript: URL.
  2. Boundary: Value is written raw via innerHTML or unescaped template interpolation.
  3. Sink: Browser parser executes injected script inside the victim's origin and session.
01 Untrusted Input

02 Context Encoder + CSP
Verified
03 Inert DOM Text
  1. Source: Untrusted input arrives from the request, storage, or URL.
  2. Boundary: Output is encoded for the exact context (textContent / safe HTML sanitizer) and guarded by CSP.
  3. Sink: Browser displays literal characters; inline script execution is blocked.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A cryptographic random number generator should be indistinguishable from random to an observer who has seen no previous outputs.
  • Operating system generators are seeded from hardware entropy sources and are suitable for keys, nonces and salts.
  • A general-purpose random function in a programming language is often predictable, and was the root cause of many real vulnerabilities.
  • A nonce must be unique for a given key, which is a different requirement from being random, and is usually easier to guarantee.
  • A unique nonce can be a counter, and a counter is easier to reason about than a random value you hope does not collide.

The background

  • Early software seeded generators with the current time, which made keys guessable to anyone who knew roughly when the system booted.
  • A small change in initialisation values in a widely used cryptography library had an outsized effect, and the incident changed how randomness is reviewed.
  • Randomness requirements became formal, with standards specifying how randomness should be obtained and tested.
  • Hardware and virtualised environments made accidental weak entropy easier to introduce, since a virtual machine can start repeatedly from similar state.

Real-world examples

  • Predictable session identifiers let an attacker fix a session before a victim ever logs in, which is why session generation is security-critical.
  • A virtual machine restored from a snapshot can start with the same generator state, so keys created after a restore can repeat.
  • Predictable password-reset tokens turn a forgotten password into an account takeover.

What to look for

  • Check that keys, nonces, tokens and identifiers all come from a cryptographic source, not a general-purpose one.
  • Look for time-based seeding anywhere a value must be unpredictable.
  • Check whether nonces are guaranteed unique or merely random, and prefer uniqueness.
  • Look for a fork, restore or snapshot path that could reproduce generator state.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Applying the repetition-count health test described in the recommendation to a stream you generate yourself, then interpreting what a triggered test would tell you about the source feeding your keys

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Use the operating system or a vetted library for every security-relevant random value.
  • Prefer counters or explicit uniqueness guarantees for nonces where the construction allows it.
  • Reseed appropriately after virtual machine snapshot or restore operations.
  • Treat any code that rolls its own random generator as unsafe until proven otherwise.
  • Use constant-time comparisons for values compared against attacker input, since a timing difference leaks information.
